newsitem.title: USA: Gene defect may redirect Alzheimer's research.
newsitem.headline: Gene defect may redirect Alzheimer's research.

text.p: A defect in the energy-producing machinery of a cell may be linked to Alzheimer's disease, a finding that could lead to understanding and treating the debilitating dementia, scientists said on Monday.

In Tuesday's edition of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers reported that they discovered a genetic effect in the part of the cell called the mitochondria. It affects how the brain cells break down glucose, or sugar, and turn it into energy.

The abnormality may generate too many free radicals, which can kill brain cells, according to the team of researchers from the San Diego-based Mitokor company, the University of Virginia, Harvard, and the University of California at San Diego.
The abnormality in the cell metabolism may also explain the other telltale signs of Alzheimer's, the plaques and tangles that form in the brain.

"This is a potentially very important new piece of fundamental information about how Alzheimer's disease puts brain cells at risk," said Zaven Khachaturian, a scientist who directs the Alzheimer's Association's Ronald and Nancy Reagan Research Institute.

MitoKor president Robert Davis said in a statement the scientists found mutations in mitochondrial DNA that affect two units of an enzyme called cytochrome c oxidase. That enzyme activity is decreased in the brains of Alzheimer's patients, who develop the disease late in life.

The researchers removed the mitochondrial DNA from cells in lab experiments and replaced it with the mitochondrial DNA from Alzheimer's patients. The cultured cells then exhibited some signs of the disease.
MitoKor officials said they have used this finding to develop a diagnostic tool that drug companies can use to test experimental therapies.
"We plan on ultimately making this assay available for use as a confirmation of the clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer's," said MitoKor vice president Michele LeGear.
About four million Americans have Alzheimer's disease, including former President Reagan. There is no cure for the degenerative disorder.
